Action Plan:
1. Occupational hand dermatitis: patient to wear protective gloves at all times when using cleaning products.  
2. Dispense topical corticosteroid cream (potency, dose, and frequency not documented) – prescription sent electronically to patient’s pharmacy.  
3. Dispense a high-oil-content emollient (brand/strength not documented); patient instructed to apply a thick layer to both palms 3–4 times daily for 10–14 days.  
4. Review: if no significant improvement by day 10–14, or if symptoms worsen/spread, patient to re-attend earlier for reassessment and possible alternative therapy.  
5. Work advice: may remain off work until pain allows functional use of hands; must use gloves on return.  
6. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Reason for visit: 3–4-month history of painful, itchy, cracked skin on both palms; worsened over past few days, now limiting ability to work.  
• Associated symptoms: intermittent itch; occasional bleeding only when scratched; denies fever, nausea, vomiting, bowel or urinary changes.  
• Past medical history: Type 2 diabetes.  
• Medications:  
  – Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented)  
  – OTC E45 cream (no benefit)  
  – OTC antihistamine (name/dose not documented; no benefit)  
• Allergies: none known.  
• Family history: diabetes.  
• Social history:  
  – Occupation: hotel housekeeper; frequent exposure to cleaning chemicals; inconsistent glove use.  
  – Smoking: none.  
  – Alcohol: “a couple of pints” per week.  

Objective:
• No physical examination findings documented (telephone consultation).  
• No vitals or investigations available.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Hand dermatitis (likely irritant/contact):
   – Assessment: Occupational contact dermatitis of both palms.  
   – Differential: Eczema, psoriasis, tinea manuum.  
   – Investigations planned: none at this stage.  
   – Treatment: topical corticosteroid cream (dose/frequency not documented); high-potency emollient 3–4×/day; advice to avoid chemical irritants and wear gloves.  
   – Referrals: none currently; consider dermatology referral if poor response.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: physical exam, vitals, steroid potency/dose/frequency, exact emollient name/strength.  
● Internal conflicts: none noted.  
● Transcript quality: clear audio; minimal background noise; occasional minor speech overlap but clinically understandable.
